mn76:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
mn76:2.1: Now on that occasion Sandaka the Wanderer was staying in the Pilakkha-tree Cave together with a large assembly of about five hundred wanderers.
mn76:3.1: Then when it was evening, the venerable Ānanda rose from meditation and addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn76:3.2: “Come, friends, let us go to the Rain Pool to see the cave.”
mn76:3.3: “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the venerable Ānanda.
mn76:3.4: Then the venerable Ānanda went to the Rain Pool together with a number of bhikkhus.
mn76:4.1: Now on that occasion Sandaka the Wanderer was sitting together with a large assembly of wanderers who were shouting and making a great uproar and noise, talking many kinds of pointless talk,[^1] such as:
mn76:4.2: talk of kings, talk of robbers, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drink, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of scents, talk of relatives, talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of countries, talk of women, talk of heroes, talk of streets, talk of wells, talk of the departed, various idle tales, speculation about the world, speculation about the sea, talk of whether things are or are not, and so on.
mn76:4.3: Sandaka the Wanderer saw the venerable Ānanda coming in the distance.
mn76:4.4: Seeing him, he quieted his own assembly:
mn76:4.5: “Be quiet, sirs, do not make a noise;
mn76:4.6: here comes the ascetic Ānanda, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
mn76:4.7: Of those disciples of the ascetic Gotama who are staying at Kosambī, this ascetic Ānanda is one.
mn76:4.8: Those venerable ones like quiet, are trained in quiet, and speak in praise of quiet;
mn76:4.9: perhaps, finding our assembly quiet, he will think it fit to approach.”
mn76:5.1: Then the venerable Ānanda went up to Sandaka the Wanderer.
mn76:5.2: Sandaka the Wanderer said to the venerable Ānanda:
mn76:5.3: “Let Master Ānanda come; welcome to Master Ānanda.
mn76:5.4: It is long, Master Ānanda, since you made an occasion to come here.
mn76:5.5: Let Master Ānanda be seated; this seat is ready.”
mn76:5.6: The venerable Ānanda sat down on the seat made ready.
mn76:5.7: And Sandaka the Wanderer took a certain low seat and sat down at one side.
mn76:5.8: The venerable Ānanda then said to Sandaka the Wanderer, as he sat at one side:
mn76:5.9: “What talk are you gathered here for now, Sandaka? And what was your discussion that was left unfinished?”
mn76:5.10: “Let that be, Master Ānanda, this talk for which we are now gathered here.
mn76:5.11: It will not be hard for Master Ānanda to hear about it later too.
mn76:5.12: It would be good if a talk on the Dhamma in his own teacher’s tradition should occur to Master Ānanda himself.”
mn76:5.13: “Well then, Sandaka, listen and attend closely to what I shall say.”
mn76:5.14: “Yes, sir,” Sandaka the Wanderer replied to the venerable Ānanda.
mn76:6.1: “Sandaka, these four kinds of life that are not the life divine have been declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, and these four kinds of life divine without consolation have also been declared, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”
mn76:6.2: “But, Master Ānanda, what are those four kinds of life that are not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma?”
mn76:7.1: “Here, Sandaka, a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:
mn76:7.2: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declared this world and the other world, who have travelled the right path and practised rightly.[^2]
mn76:7.3: This person is made up of the four great elements, and when he dies, the earth in him returns and goes back to the body of earth, the water returns and goes back to the body of water, the fire returns and goes back to the body of fire, the air returns and goes back to the body of air, and the faculties pass over into space.
mn76:7.4: Four men, with the bier as the fifth, carry the corpse away;
mn76:7.5: eulogies are spoken only as far as the charnel ground;
mn76:7.8: giving is a doctrine fabricated by fools.
mn76:7.9: The talk of those who assert there is something is empty, false chatter.
mn76:7.10: Both fools and the wise, at the breaking up of the body, are annihilated, perish, and do not exist after death.’
mn76:8.1: “About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:
mn76:8.2: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—
mn76:8.3: there is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have themselves realized by direct knowledge and declared this world and the other world, who have travelled the right path and practised rightly.
mn76:8.4: This person is made up of the four great elements, and when he dies, the earth in him returns and goes back to the body of earth, the water returns and goes back to the body of water, the fire returns and goes back to the body of fire, the air returns and goes back to the body of air, and the faculties pass over into space.
mn76:8.5: Four men, with the bier as the fifth, carry the corpse away; eulogies are spoken only as far as the charnel ground.
mn76:8.8: giving is a doctrine fabricated by fools.
mn76:8.9: The talk of those who assert there is something is empty, false chatter.
mn76:8.10: Both fools and the wise, at the breaking up of the body, are annihilated, perish, and do not exist after death.’
mn76:8.11: If this good teacher’s word is true, then, without having done anything, I have done what had to be done here; without having lived the life, I have lived it here.
mn76:8.12: Both of us are equal here, having attained the ascetic life, in that I do not say: ‘Both of us, at the breaking up of the body, will be annihilated, will perish, and will not exist after death.’
mn76:8.13: But this good teacher’s going naked, shaving his head, his squatting posture as a practice, and the plucking out of his hair and beard, are all superfluous—for I, living at home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, accepting gold and silver, shall have exactly the same destination in the life to come as this good teacher.
mn76:8.14: So what do I know, what do I see, that I should live the life divine under this teacher?
mn76:8.16: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.
mn76:9.1: This, Sandaka, is the first kind of life that is not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:10.1: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:
mn76:10.2: ‘For one who acts or causes others to act, for one who mutilates or causes others to mutilate, for one who tortures or causes others to torture, for one who inflicts sorrow or causes others to inflict sorrow, for one who oppresses or causes others to oppress, for one who intimidates or causes others to intimidate, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, waylays highways, commits adultery, speaks falsehood—no evil is done by the doer.
mn76:10.3: Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make all the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.
mn76:10.4: Even if one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and causing others to kill, mutilating and causing others to mutilate, torturing and causing others to torture, there would be no evil resulting from that, no coming of evil.
mn76:10.5: Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and causing others to give, offering sacrifice and causing others to offer sacrifice, there would be no merit resulting from that, no coming of merit.
mn76:10.6: By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit, no coming of merit.’
mn76:11.1: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:
mn76:11.2: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—
mn76:11.3: for one who acts or causes others to act, for one who mutilates or causes others to mutilate, for one who tortures or causes others to torture, for one who inflicts sorrow or causes others to inflict sorrow, for one who oppresses or causes others to oppress, for one who intimidates or causes others to intimidate, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders wealth, commits burglary, waylays highways, commits adultery, speaks falsehood—no evil is done by the doer. mn76:11.5: Even if one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and causing others to give, offering sacrifice and causing others to offer sacrifice, there would be no merit resulting from that, no coming of merit.
mn76:11.6: By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit, no coming of merit.’

mn76:13.1: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:
mn76:13.2: ‘There is no cause, no condition, for the defilement of beings;
mn76:13.3: beings are defiled without cause or condition;
mn76:13.4: there is no cause, no condition, for the purification of beings;
mn76:13.5: beings are purified without cause or condition;
mn76:13.6: there is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly effort;
mn76:13.7: all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy; shaped by destiny, circumstance, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes.’
mn76:14.1: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:
mn76:14.2: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—
mn76:14.3: there is no cause, no condition, for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition.
mn76:14.4: There is no cause, no condition, for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition.
mn76:14.5: There is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly effort; all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy; shaped by destiny, circumstance, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes.’

mn76:14.8: But this good teacher’s going naked, shaving his head, his squatting posture as a practice, and the plucking out of his hair and beard, are all superfluous—for I, living at home crowded with children, enjoying Kāsi sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, accepting gold and silver, shall have exactly the same destination in the life to come as this good teacher.

mn76:16.1: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher has this doctrine and this view:
mn76:16.2: ‘There are these seven bodies that are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar;
mn76:16.3: they do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another, and are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.
mn76:16.5: The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the soul as the seventh—
mn76:16.6: these seven bodies are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar.
mn76:16.7: They do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another, and are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.
mn76:16.8: Herein there is no slayer nor one who causes slaying, no hearer nor one who causes hearing, no cognizer nor one who causes cognizing.
mn76:16.9: Even one who cuts off another’s head with a sharp sword does not deprive anyone of life;
mn76:16.10: the sword simply passes through the gap between the seven bodies.
mn76:16.11: There are, moreover, fourteen hundred thousand principal wombs, and six thousand more, and six hundred more; five hundred kinds of action, and five kinds of action, and three kinds of action; a kind of action and a half-kind of action; sixty-two paths; sixty-two sub-aeons; six classes; eight stages of man; four thousand nine hundred kinds of livelihood; four thousand nine hundred kinds of wanderers; four thousand nine hundred abodes of nāgas; two thousand faculties; three thousand hells; thirty-six elements of dust; seven percipient wombs; seven non-percipient wombs; seven wombless wombs; seven kinds of gods; seven kinds of humans; seven kinds of demons; seven lakes; seven knots; seven precipices; seven hundred precipices; seven dreams; seven hundred dreams; and eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons through which, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.[^9]
mn76:16.12: Herein there is no such thing as: “By this virtue, or this observance, or this austerity, or this life divine, I shall ripen unripened action, or, by repeatedly experiencing it, exhaust ripened action.”
mn76:16.13: Pleasure and pain are meted out as by a measure, and the round of rebirths has a fixed limit; there is no decrease or increase, no rising or falling.
mn76:16.14: Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds itself as it runs;
mn76:16.15: so too, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.’
mn76:17.1: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:
mn76:17.2: ‘This good teacher has this doctrine and this view—
mn76:17.3: there are these seven bodies that are not made, not made of anything made, not created, not caused to be created, barren, standing firm like a mountain-peak, standing firm like a pillar.
mn76:17.4: They do not move, do not change, do not obstruct one another.
mn76:17.5: They are not able to cause one another pleasure or pain or both.
mn76:17.7: The earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the air-body, pleasure, pain, and the soul as the seventh—

mn76:17.12: Even one who cuts off another’s head with a sharp sword does not deprive anyone of life;

mn76:17.15: Herein there is no such thing as: “By this virtue, or this observance, or this austerity, or this life divine, I shall ripen unripened action, or, by repeatedly experiencing it, exhaust ripened action.” Pleasure and pain are meted out as by a measure, and the round of rebirths has a fixed limit; there is no decrease or increase, no rising or falling.
mn76:17.16: Just as a ball of thread, when thrown, unwinds itself as it runs;
mn76:17.17: so too, running on and wandering on, fools and the wise alike will make an end of suffering.’

mn76:19.1: These, Sandaka, are the four kinds of life that are not the life divine, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”
mn76:20.1: “It is wonderful, Master Ānanda, it is marvellous, Master Ānanda,
mn76:20.2: how these four kinds of life that are actually not the life divine have been declared as ‘not the life divine’ by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:20.3: But, Master Ānanda, what are those four kinds of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma?”
mn76:21.1: “Here, Sandaka, a certain teacher claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision thus:
mn76:21.2: ‘Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are continuously and unceasingly present to me.’
mn76:21.3: He enters an empty house, gets no almsfood, is bitten by a dog, meets a fierce elephant, meets a fierce horse, meets a fierce ox, asks the name and clan of a woman or a man, asks the name of a village or town and the way to it.[^4]
mn76:21.4: When asked: ‘Why is that?’[^3] he says: ‘I had to enter an empty house, that is why I entered it; I was not to get almsfood, that is why I did not get it; I had to be bitten by a dog, that is why I was bitten; I had to meet a fierce elephant, that is why I met it; I had to meet a fierce horse, that is why I met it; I had to meet a fierce ox, that is why I met it; I had to ask the name and clan of a woman or a man, that is why I asked; I had to ask the name of a village or town and the way to it, that is why I asked.’
mn76:22.1: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:
mn76:22.2: ‘This good teacher claims to be omniscient and all-seeing, professing complete knowledge and vision … “I had to ask the name of a village or town and the way to it, that is why I asked.”’
mn76:22.4: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.
mn76:23.1: This, Sandaka, is the first kind of life divine without consolation, declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, wherein a wise man would certainly not live the life divine, or, if he did live it, he would not succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:24.1: “Again, Sandaka, here a certain teacher relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth.[^5]
mn76:24.2: He teaches a Dhamma by oral tradition, by legend handed down from generation to generation, by what has come down in the scriptures.
mn76:24.3: But for a teacher who relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth, some things are well remembered and some are badly remembered, and some are so and some are otherwise.[^6]
mn76:25.1: About this, Sandaka, a wise man considers thus:
mn76:25.2: ‘This good teacher relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth, and teaches a Dhamma by oral tradition, by legend handed down from generation to generation, by what has come down in the scriptures.
mn76:25.3: But for a teacher who relies on oral tradition, holding oral tradition as truth, some things are well remembered and some are badly remembered, and some are so and some are otherwise.’
mn76:25.5: knowing this, he becomes disenchanted with that life divine and departs from it.

mn76:27.3: But for a teacher who is a rationalist, an investigator, some things are well reasoned and some are badly reasoned, and some are so and some are otherwise.

mn76:30.3: ‘I don’t say it is so; I don’t say it is thus; I don’t say it is otherwise; I don’t say it is not so; nor do I say it is not not so.’

mn76:34.3: But, Master Ānanda, what does that Teacher assert, what does he declare, wherein a wise man would certainly live the life divine, and, living it, would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma?”
mn76:35-42.1: “Here, Sandaka, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed …
mn76:35-42.2: … having abandoned these five hindrances, defilements of mind that weaken wisdom,
mn76:35-42.3: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn76:35-42.4: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:43.1: Again, Sandaka, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …
mn76:43.2: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:44-45.1: Again, Sandaka, with the fading away of joy as well, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity … and enters upon and abides in the third jhāna …
mn76:44-45.2: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:46.1: Again, Sandaka, with the abandoning of pleasure … a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna …
mn76:46.2: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:47.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
mn76:47.2: He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births … thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
mn76:47.3: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:48.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
mn76:48.2: With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.
mn76:48.3: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.
mn76:49.1: When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it, inclines it, to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.
mn76:49.2: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’;
mn76:49.3: he understands as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
mn76:50.1: Knowing and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, liberated from the taint of being, liberated from the taint of ignorance.
mn76:50.2: When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’
mn76:50.3: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn76:50.4: When a wise man attains such a sublime distinction under any teacher, he would certainly live the life divine under him, and, living it, he would succeed in the true method, the wholesome Dhamma.”
mn76:51.1: “But, Master Ānanda, would a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—would he indulge in sensual pleasures?”
mn76:51.2: “Sandaka, a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in five instances.
mn76:51.3: A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted is incapable of deliberately depriving a living being of life; he is incapable of taking what is not given in the manner of theft; he is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse; he is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie; he is incapable of storing up goods for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, as he formerly did as a householder.
mn76:51.4: A bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing in these five instances.”
mn76:52.1: “But, Master Ānanda, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is the knowledge and vision continuously and unceasingly present to him, whether he is walking or standing, asleep or awake, that:
mn76:52.3: “Well then, Sandaka, I shall give you a simile;
mn76:52.4: for by means of a simile some wise men here understand the meaning of what is said.
mn76:52.5: Suppose, Sandaka, a man’s hands and feet were cut off;[^10]
mn76:52.6: would he, whether walking or standing, asleep or awake, continuously and unceasingly know:
mn76:52.7: ‘my hands and feet are cut off,’ or would he know it only when he reviews the fact:
mn76:52.8: ‘my hands and feet are cut off’?”
mn76:52.9: “That man, Master Ānanda, does not continuously and unceasingly know:
mn76:52.10: ‘my hands and feet are cut off.’
mn76:52.11: Rather, he knows it when he reviews the fact:
mn76:52.12: ‘my hands and feet are cut off.’”
mn76:52.13: “So too, Sandaka, for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant with the taints exhausted, who has lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, destroyed the fetters of being, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, the knowledge and vision is not continuously and unceasingly present to him, whether he is walking or standing, asleep or awake, that:
mn76:52.15: rather, he knows it when he reviews the fact:
mn76:53.1: “But, Master Ānanda, how many guides[^7] are there in this Dhamma and Discipline?”
mn76:53.2: “There are not just one hundred, Sandaka, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but far more than that, who are guides in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
mn76:53.3: “It is wonderful, Master Ānanda, it is marvellous, Master Ānanda.
mn76:53.4: There will be no extolling of one’s own doctrine, no disparaging of others’ doctrines, but the teaching of the Dhamma will be within its proper scope, and yet so many guides are seen.
mn76:53.5: But these Ājīvaka ascetics, mothers’ dead sons,[^8] both extol themselves and disparage others, and yet they proclaim only three guides, namely:
mn76:53.6: Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla.”
mn76:54.1: Then Sandaka the Wanderer addressed his own assembly:
mn76:54.2: “Sirs, go and live the life divine under the ascetic Gotama.
mn76:54.3: It is not easy now for us to give up gain, honour, and fame.”
mn76:54.4: So Sandaka the Wanderer sent his own assembly to live the life divine under the Blessed One.
